intros.market: Five certificate authorities control 88% of global issuance, with Internet Security Research Group at 32%, Google Trust Services at 21%, and DigiCert at 18%. The three-CA concentration ratio stands at 71%, yielding an HHI of 1980, well above the 1500 threshold economists consider highly concentrated. Despite this consolidation at the top, 88 CAs hold trusted roots across the four major browser stores, creating a long tail of 74 lower-volume operators with full trust capabilities.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four simultaneously, while 142 roots exist exclusively in Microsoft's store. Just 38 CA owners hold roots in all four programs, fragmenting the trust landscape browser by browser. This disagreement forces certificate subscribers to navigate per-store inclusion decisions and complicates chain-building logic, as a validation path trusted in Edge may fail in Chrome or Safari.
intros.conc: The top three CAs issue 71% of all certificates, pushing the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index to 1980, a level that signals high market concentration and systemic dependency risk. If any of these operators suffered a compromise or operational failure, a substantial portion of the web would face immediate certificate replacement pressure. The 74 tail CAs collectively hold less than 12% share but retain identical trust store privileges, creating asymmetric risk exposure across the ecosystem.
intros.tail: 74 certificate authorities each issue less than 1% of global volume yet hold the same trust store inclusion as the top-five operators who control 88% of issuance. These tail CAs represent the full scope of compliance and operational risk without the scale, automation, or oversight attention that follows high-volume issuers. A single misissuance from a low-volume operator carries identical browser trust and can trigger the same incident response machinery as a failure from a major CA.
intros.geo: United States-based CAs issue 93% of all trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of the 88 trusted authorities, while Europe's 44 CAs collectively issue just 7%. Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs account for less than 0.1% of issuance, creating a concentration profile where a small number of US corporations dominate global certificate supply. This geographic imbalance means regulatory or legal changes in US jurisdiction can reshape the entire WebPKI surface, independent of where subscribers or relying parties operate.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned certificate authorities hold trusted roots, though they collectively issue just 0.09% of certificates. These operators span jurisdictions with varying transparency norms and legal frameworks, raising questions about oversight mechanisms when incidents occur. The low issuance share does not reduce the systemic risk, as each government CA retains full authority to issue for any domain within its trust scope.
intros.jurisdiction: Five high-risk jurisdictions hold trusted CAs where legal frameworks permit compelled certificate issuance, surveillance mandates, or extraterritorial data access: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey are classified as moderate risk based on evolving legal powers and historical governance posture. These jurisdictions collectively host CAs capable of issuing for domains outside their borders, creating a legal and operational surface that extends beyond the 93% US issuance concentration noted in geographic distribution.
intros.ops: 1,793 incidents across 55 CAs have been disclosed since formal tracking began, with misissuance (683) and governance failures (591) representing the two largest categories. CAs self-detect only 32% of incidents, while external researchers and automated tools account for 32% combined, revealing a material surveillance gap in operator monitoring. Policy failures (263), disclosure failures (164), and audit findings (110) show that compliance breakdowns occur across the full lifecycle of detection, reporting, and remediation.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture tab examines root certificate algorithms, key sizes, and standards compliance across the 335 trusted roots, measuring adherence to current baseline requirements and readiness for post-quantum transitions. This layer of risk intersects with the long tail problem, as lower-volume CAs may lack the engineering resources to rotate roots or deploy algorithm agility at the pace set by high-volume operators. No specific cryptographic vulnerabilities are evident in the current data snapshot, but the distributed governance model means upgrade timelines vary significantly by CA owner.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across all root programs, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures and 10 following a pattern of repeated issues. The posture distribution shows seven cases of negligent noncompliance, three of demonstrated incompetence, and three of willful circumvention, indicating that most distrust stems from operational breakdown rather than malicious intent. The median runway from distrust announcement to root removal is 1,185 days, granting CAs nearly three years to wind down issuance while subscribers migrate certificates.
intros.policy: Of 43 active TLS issuers measured, only nine are operationally ready to issue at the 47-day validity limit set for March 2029, while three remain at risk of non-compliance with the 200-day threshold arriving in March 2026. This readiness gap exists as the regulatory surface CAs must navigate has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations, with 76% classified as mandatory across CA/B Forum baseline requirements, root program policies, and audit criteria. The compliance complexity compounds the operational challenge, as CAs must track obligations across multiple governing bodies while simultaneously re-engineering issuance and renewal flows to meet compressed validity windows.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has declined sharply from 2019, when Chrome reviewed 68% of incidents and Mozilla 78%, to 2025 when Chrome covered just 18% and Mozilla 10%. Apple's 5% coverage and Microsoft's 0% participation in formal incident review leave most of the 223 incidents from 2025 without substantive root program response. This collapse in oversight occurs even as Chrome's governance corpus reaches 741 bugs with 296 substantive interventions, suggesting that formal incident review no longer reflects actual program activity.
intros.community: 56 CA/B Forum members exist on paper, but only 21 contribute actively to ballot proposals, endorsements, or working group output, leaving 35 organizations with zero recorded participation. Sectigo leads organizational ballot activity, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually, far outpacing the second-most-active participant. This silent majority pattern means a small core of contributors shapes baseline requirements and operational policy on behalf of the entire 88-CA trust surface, concentrating governance influence among operators who also control market share.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 28% of in-scope incidents when measured against their corresponding audit periods, meaning clean audit letters coexist with real incident histories documented in public bug trackers. 38 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter dates and actual disclosure timing, while six letters contain qualified opinions flagging scope limitations or unresolved findings. 63.7% of WebTrust and 70.6% of ETSI letters are self-reported by CAs rather than published directly by auditors, creating a disclosure chain vulnerable to selective timing or omission.
